chapter_title: Introduction to Kanban: Principles and Core Practices
chapter_summary:
Welcome to our journey into Kanban, a powerful methodology for visualizing work, limiting work in progress, and maximizing efficiency. While often associated with software development, Kanban's roots lie in the Toyota Production System, specifically in the concept of "just-in-time" manufacturing. Taiichi Ohno, a pioneer at Toyota, developed a system to optimize the flow of materials and information, ensuring that components were only produced when needed, thereby reducing waste and improving throughput. This lean manufacturing philosophy, focused on continuous improvement and eliminating waste, forms the bedrock of modern Kanban. Unlike Scrum, which prescribes specific roles, ceremonies, and time-boxed iterations, Kanban is a method for evolving your existing process incrementally. It's less about revolution and more about continuous, evolutionary change, making it highly adaptable to various contexts, from software teams to marketing departments and even personal task management.

At its heart, Kanban is guided by four foundational principles that emphasize respect for the current state and a commitment to continuous improvement. The first principle is **"Start with what you do now."** This means you don't need to discard your existing processes, roles, or responsibilities to adopt Kanban. Instead, you begin by understanding your current workflow, visualizing it, and then incrementally improving it. This approach minimizes resistance and allows for a smoother transition. The second principle, **"Agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change,"** reinforces this idea. Kanban advocates for small, continuous adjustments rather than large, disruptive overhauls. This reduces risk and allows teams to experiment and learn without destabilizing their operations. The third principle, **"Respect current processes, roles, and responsibilities,"** acknowledges the value of existing knowledge and experience within an organization. Kanban doesn't dictate new roles but rather encourages individuals to contribute to process improvement within their current capacities. Finally, **"Encourage acts of leadership at all levels"** promotes a culture where everyone is empowered to identify opportunities for improvement and take initiative, fostering a sense of collective ownership and continuous learning.

Beyond these principles, Kanban is put into practice through six core practices that guide its implementation. The first and most visible practice is **"Visualize the workflow."** This typically involves a Kanban board, which uses cards to represent work items and columns to represent different stages of the workflow. By making all work visible, teams can easily see the status of tasks, identify bottlenecks, and understand the overall flow. The second crucial practice is **"Limit Work In Progress (WIP)."** This means setting explicit limits on the number of items that can be in progress at any given stage of the workflow. The goal is to prevent multitasking, improve focus, and reduce the time it takes for a single work item to complete its journey. Think of it like a highway with too many cars – limiting WIP is like ensuring the road doesn't get jammed, allowing traffic to flow smoothly.

The third practice, **"Manage flow,"** focuses on ensuring that work moves through the system as smoothly and predictably as possible. This involves actively monitoring the movement of work items, identifying and addressing blockages, and continuously optimizing the process to reduce lead time and cycle time. The fourth practice is **"Make process policies explicit."** This means clearly defining the rules and guidelines for how work moves through each stage of the Kanban board. For example, what criteria must be met for a task to move from "Development" to "Testing"? Explicit policies reduce ambiguity, ensure consistency, and enable everyone to understand and adhere to the process. A common mistake here is having implicit rules that only a few team members understand, leading to confusion and inefficiencies.

The fifth practice, **"Implement feedback loops,"** is vital for continuous learning and adaptation. Kanban encourages various feedback mechanisms, such as daily stand-ups focused on flow, service delivery reviews with customers, and operations reviews to analyze system performance. These loops provide opportunities to inspect the process, gather data, and identify areas for improvement. Finally, **"Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally"** emphasizes the iterative and data-driven nature of Kanban. Teams are encouraged to use metrics and observations to propose and test small changes, learning from the results and continuously refining their process. This scientific approach to improvement ensures that changes are based on evidence rather than assumptions. By embracing these principles and practices, teams can transform their workflow into a highly efficient, responsive, and continuously improving system.

screens.title: Introduction to Kanban: Principles & Core Practices
screens.subtitle: Visualize work, limit WIP, and build continuous improvement into how you deliver value.

narration.text: Welcome. In this short module we’ll trace Kanban from its roots in lean manufacturing to the practical practices teams use today. Kanban began as a way to manage parts on a production line so nothing was built before it was needed. That lean impulse—reduce waste and make flow predictable—translates cleanly to knowledge work. You’ll learn four guiding principles that make Kanban a gentle, evolutionary approach and six core practices that bring those principles to life: visualize work, limit work in progress, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, and improve collaboratively. Each idea here is practical: we’ll map the principles to real examples like a personal weekly Kanban board and a software team fixing a bottleneck. Pay attention to common mistakes, because Kanban is often misunderstood as a lightweight, one-size-fits-all tool. It’s not about absence of discipline; it’s about making discipline visible and testable. By the end you’ll be able to sketch a simple Kanban board, set sensible WIP limits, and suggest one small experiment your team can run this week. Think about a recent week of work—what clogged your flow—and we’ll design a small change to improve it.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Kanban helps teams make work visible, limit concurrent work, and continuously improve the flow of value without forcing roles or ceremonies.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand where Kanban comes from and why it emphasizes flow over fixed roles. You will be able to name and explain the four Kanban principles and show how each principle guides change in a real team. You will identify and describe the six core practices that turn those principles into everyday habits: how to create a visible board, why WIP limits matter, ways to manage flow, the importance of explicit policies, what feedback loops to run, and how to test changes experimentally. You will also learn to distinguish Kanban from other agile approaches, in particular that Kanban evolves the current process rather than replacing it with mandated ceremonies. Finally, you will practice designing a simple personal Kanban board and setting a WIP limit so you can try an experiment this week. These are practical skills: you will be able to sketch a board, set a WIP value, run a short flow-focused stand-up, and propose a single small improvement to measure.

keyIdea.title: Objectives
keyIdea.text: Master the principles and practices so you can apply Kanban to personal work or a team process with one small experiment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Assessment
screens.subtitle: How you will practice and verify each skill

narration.text: This page maps the objectives to hands-on practice and quick assessment ideas. First, to prove you understand origins and philosophy, sketch a short paragraph linking just-in-time manufacturing to visualizing work in knowledge tasks. Second, to show mastery of principles, describe a team scenario where you would avoid wholesale change and instead try small experiments. Third, for the practices, design or list a Kanban board with explicit WIP limits and an example policy for moving an item to the next stage. Fourth, to verify your applied skill, build a personal board with five tasks and set a Doing WIP limit of two, then run a two-day simulation and note what caused blockage. Each assessment is evidence-focused: it demonstrates understanding through artifacts you create, not just a multiple choice answer. When you run these small experiments, measure one thing—lead time or how long an item takes to finish—so your next change can be data driven. This skill mapping helps you move from described concepts to concrete, low-risk experiments you can run in real teams.

screens.title: Origins: Toyota, Just-in-Time, and Lean
screens.subtitle: How an assembly-line idea became a method for knowledge work

narration.text: Kanban’s story begins in manufacturing, specifically with the Toyota Production System and the goal of just-in-time delivery. In that context, a kanban card signalled that a part was needed and prevented overproduction. The core lesson for knowledge work is the same: don’t create more work than the system can absorb. Lean manufacturing introduced the idea of eliminating waste—activities that don’t add value—and of smoothing flow so throughput becomes predictable. Translating this to a software or office team, a Kanban board is the visible equivalent of the assembly line: it shows work items, stages, and where items pile up. A concrete example: in a busy restaurant kitchen before Kanban, cooks might start many dishes at once, causing long waits for plating. Using a pull signal and limits, the kitchen focuses on finishing a few dishes completely before starting more, which shortens delivery time. A common misconception is to believe Kanban removes planning; it does not. It makes planning and capacity explicit so teams can prioritize and decide when to pull more work. The practical takeaway: by making inventory and work visible and constrained, Kanban turns vague overload into measurable signals you can act on.

keyIdea.title: Historical link
keyIdea.text: Kanban adapts just-in-time thinking to make knowledge work visible, limited, and measurable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Origins
Definition

Toyota, JIT, and the lean root of Kanban

Kanban began as a signal-based pull system that prevented overproduction and reduced waste. The same pull idea helps knowledge teams avoid starting more work than they can finish.

Concrete example
A restaurant kitchen switches from starting many plates to finishing a small number before taking new orders, reducing wait time—equivalent to limiting WIP.
Why it matters
Making inventory visible transforms hidden bottlenecks into actionable signals for improvement and predictable delivery.
Common misconception
Kanban is not the absence of process. It reveals the process so you can improve it deliberately.
Analogy
Imagine a conveyor of tasks visible at all times. Each task is a card. Too many cards create queues and wait time. Kanban introduces signals and limits so the conveyor flows smoothly.
Pull signal
Work is pulled only when capacity exists downstream.
Visible inventory
Cards show active items and where they are stuck.
Key Takeaway

Kanban transfers just-in-time thinking to knowledge work: make work visible, limit it, and improve flow.

screens.title: Kanban vs Scrum
screens.subtitle: Different approaches to agility and when to choose each

narration.text: Kanban and Scrum both aim to help teams deliver value iteratively, but they differ in prescription and change style. Scrum defines roles, ceremonies, and fixed-length sprints. It is useful when a team benefits from time-boxed planning and committed scope within iterations. Kanban, by contrast, is less prescriptive: it asks teams to visualize their current workflow, set explicit limits, and evolve the process incrementally. A clear example: a support team with unpredictable incoming requests may prefer Kanban because it allows continuous prioritization and pull-based flow. A development team working on a feature set that benefits from synchronized delivery may prefer Scrum’s sprint cadence. A common misconception is that Kanban is only for operations or that Scrum is always better for software delivery. The right choice depends on variability, need for synchronization, and how much your team wants to evolve existing roles. If you already have a process that mostly works but has bottlenecks, Kanban lets you improve without changing job titles or introducing new ceremonies. This flexibility is powerful: you can combine practices from both frameworks when needed, but always measure the effect of any change so experiments remain evidence-driven.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Scrum prescribes structure and cadence; Kanban prescribes flow-focused practices that evolve the current process incrementally.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Kanban vs Scrum
Scrum

Time-boxed and role-driven

  • Fixed-length sprints with planning and review.
  • Defined roles like Scrum Master and Product Owner.
  • Good for synchronized delivery and clear sprint commitments.
Example
A feature team coordinating releases across backend and frontend benefits from sprint boundaries and integrated planning.
Kanban

Flow-focused and evolutionary

  • No mandated roles or timeboxes; start with current process.
  • Use visibility, WIP limits, and feedback loops to improve flow.
  • Ideal for variable work and continuous delivery contexts.
Example
A support team handling unplanned tickets uses a Kanban board to pull work as capacity opens.
Key takeaway
Choose Kanban to evolve an existing process and focus on flow. Choose Scrum when cadence and synchronized planning are primary needs.
Misconception
Kanban is not weaker than Scrum; it is a different tool that emphasizes continuous, evolutionary change rather than prescriptive structure.

screens.title: The Four Principles of Kanban
screens.subtitle: Start where you are and evolve experimentally

narration.text: Kanban rests on four principles that guide how you introduce change. First: start with what you do now. This reduces resistance by keeping roles and processes intact while making the workflow visible. Second: agree to pursue incremental, evolutionary change. Small experiments reduce risk and let teams learn from data. Third: respect current processes, roles, and responsibilities. Kanban assumes existing knowledge matters and uses it as the basis for improvement. Fourth: encourage acts of leadership at all levels. Improvement doesn't come only from managers; frontline contributors often see the most useful changes. A concrete scenario: a team unhappy with long review times can start by mapping their current steps, then run an experiment to limit review WIP to one pull. That small test is an incremental change that preserves roles but changes how work flows. A typical misconception is to treat these principles as optional flags: they are commitments that shape how Kanban experiments are designed and evaluated. The principle set helps teams avoid two extremes—radical reorganization and do-nothing inertia—by offering a middle path of data-driven, respectful improvement. The Four Principles of Kanban means these principles enable safe, evidence-driven change that leverages existing knowledge and distributes leadership.. In practical terms, start where you are and evolve experimentally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guiding principles
keyIdea.text: These principles enable safe, evidence-driven change that leverages existing knowledge and distributes leadership.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Four Principles
Principle 1
Start with what you do now
Observe and visualize the current flow before proposing change. This reduces friction.
Principle 2
Agree to pursue incremental change
Favor small experiments over big rewrites so you can measure impact and learn quickly.
Principle 3
Respect current roles
Use existing knowledge and authority; ask people to participate rather than replace them.
Principle 4
Encourage leadership at all levels
Frontline team members often spot the best improvements; empower them to act and experiment.
Scenario
A team maps its review steps and lets reviewers propose a WIP limit as a small experiment instead of changing roles or tools.
Key Takeaway
Principles set the tone: they favor safe, evidence-based, and inclusive improvement over top-down mandates.

screens.title: Practice Overview: The Six Core Practices
screens.subtitle: From visualization to experimental improvement

narration.text: The six core practices are the practical steps that turn Kanban principles into daily habits. First, visualize the workflow so everyone sees items and stages. Second, limit work in progress (WIP) so teams finish tasks more predictably. Third, manage flow by monitoring movement and removing blockages. Fourth, make process policies explicit so criteria for moving items are clear. Fifth, implement feedback loops—regular opportunities to inspect delivery and customer outcomes. Sixth, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally using small tests and metrics. A concrete example synthesizes these: a product team creates a visible board, sets a WIP limit of two in development, records policies for moving to testing, runs a weekly delivery review, and experiments by reallocating a tester for one sprint. The result is measurable: a reduction in average lead time. A common mistake is treating visualization as a single event—like making a board once and forgetting it. Visualization must be paired with limits and measurement to shape behavior. The practical insight is this: the practices work together, not in isolation, to make process outcomes visible, testable, and improvable. Practice Overview: The Six Core Practices means visualize, limit, manage, codify, feedback, and experiment—these six practices interlock to improve flow.. In practical terms, from visualization to experimental improvement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practices summary
keyIdea.text: Visualize, limit, manage, codify, feedback, and experiment—these six practices interlock to improve flow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Six Core Practices

Six Core Practices

These practices are applied together to convert principles into measurable change.

1. Visualize workflow
Use columns and cards to reveal work and queues.
2. Limit WIP
Set explicit caps on active items to reduce multitasking.
3. Manage flow
Monitor movement and remove blockers to improve predictability.
4. Make policies explicit
Define clear entry and exit criteria for each stage.
5. Implement feedback loops
Use reviews and operations meetings to inspect outcomes and data.
6. Improve collaboratively
Propose small experiments, measure, and learn together.
Concrete example
Create a board, set Doing WIP to two, add an explicit rule for moving to QA, run a weekly delivery review, and test reallocating one tester for a sprint. Measure lead time before and after.
Pro tip
Don’t apply practices in isolation. Visualization without WIP limits rarely changes behavior.

screens.title: Visualize the Workflow
screens.subtitle: Designing a basic Kanban board that reveals bottlenecks

narration.text: Visualizing work is the first and most visible Kanban practice. A board consists of columns representing stages and cards representing items. Start with a simple three-column board: To Do, Doing, Done. As you gain confidence, add columns like Blocked or Review, but only when you need the nuance. The purpose is to surface queues and handoffs so you can see where work piles up. A practical example: map five tasks through To Do, Doing, Blocked, and Done. When you see many cards in Blocked, that signals a dependency or a missing resource. Visualization is not decoration; it’s a diagnostic tool. One common mistake is overly granular boards with many columns that hide, rather than clarify, flow. Another mistake is forgetting to keep cards up to date. A concrete activity: draw a board on paper or in a spreadsheet, write five task cards, and simulate moving two items at a time with a WIP limit. Observe where tasks pile up and note one hypothesis—such as insufficient review capacity—to test next. The key insight is that a visible board turns abstract overload into specific, testable problems.

keyIdea.title: Visualization
keyIdea.text: A simple board makes queues visible. Use it as a diagnostic before proposing changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Visualize Workflow
Board template
Columns
  • To Do
  • Doing (consider sub-columns like In Progress / Review)
  • Done
  • Optional: Blocked, Waiting for Feedback
Card example
Study for agile exam — Owner: You — Est. 3 hours — Blocker: none
Key takeaway
Keep the board simple and live. Use it to reveal queues and trigger experiments.
Simulation activity
Steps
  1. List 5 tasks on cards and place them in To Do.
  2. Set Doing WIP limit to 2 and move two cards to Doing.
  3. If a dependency appears, move a card to Blocked and note the reason.
  4. Complete a card and move it to Done; observe lead time.
Common mistake
Adding too many columns before understanding where queues actually form.

screens.title: Limit Work In Progress (WIP)
screens.subtitle: Why limits speed delivery and how to set them

narration.text: Limiting work in progress is the practice that most directly changes team behavior. When you cap active items, you prevent context switching and reduce task handoffs that slow completion. Think of WIP limits as the effective capacity of a stage: if development can reliably handle two items at a time, setting WIP to two helps the team prioritize finishing items rather than starting new ones. A concrete example: a student sets Doing WIP to two for a week. Instead of juggling reading, coding, and errands, they focus on two tasks until one finishes. The result is decreased lead time and higher completion rate. A common misconception is to see WIP limits as arbitrary constraints. In reality, they are hypotheses: set a limit, observe cycle time and throughput, then adjust. Measuring lead time and counting how often limits are exceeded gives evidence for whether to tighten or relax a limit. When introducing WIP limits, couple them with visualization so exceeding a limit creates a visible signal that prompts discussion and investigation rather than punishment. The practice encourages teams to manage flow proactively and choose the most valuable work to finish first.

keyIdea.title: WIP limits
keyIdea.text: WIP limits reduce multitasking, reveal capacity, and produce measurable effects on lead time and throughput.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Limit WIP
What a WIP limit does
It caps active items to match team capacity, making finishing work the priority and reducing context switching.
Example: personal week
Set Doing WIP to 2. Focus on studying and the Cohortia project. You’ll likely finish more than when juggling five tasks.
How to choose a limit
  • Start small and observe cycle time.
  • Adjust based on measured throughput and team feedback.
  • Treat limits as experiments, not edicts.
Signals and behavior
When a WIP limit is reached, the team must either finish work, remove blockers, or negotiate. That visible pressure drives improvement.
Common mistake
Setting limits too low without measuring capacity, which creates constant blockers instead of learning signals.
Key takeaway
Treat WIP limits as testable constraints that reveal capacity and force finishing behavior.

screens.title: Manage Flow and Remove Blockers
screens.subtitle: Observe movement, measure lead time, and act on bottlenecks

narration.text: Managing flow is about paying attention to how work moves and making deliberate interventions to improve throughput. Flow is measured by lead time—the time from when work starts to when it finishes—and by cycle time for stages. Start by collecting simple data: record when a card enters Doing and when it reaches Done. Use this to compute average lead time and to spot outliers. If you notice many items stuck in Review, that suggests a capacity issue in testing or ambiguous exit criteria. A concrete example: a team measured a long tail of review items; they experimented by assigning a rotating reviewer and shortening review WIP. After a sprint, average lead time dropped. A common misconception is equating activity with flow; lots of started items that are not completed do not indicate progress. Flow asks you to value finished work. When you identify a bottleneck, frame an experiment: change one variable such as WIP, swap a role temporarily, or clarify a policy. Then measure the effect and iterate. The discipline of measuring before and after turns opinions into evidence, which is the backbone of experimental improvement.

keyIdea.title: Manage flow
keyIdea.text: Measure lead time, identify bottlenecks, and run small experiments to improve throughput.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Manage Flow
What to measure
  • Lead time: start to finish for an item.
  • Cycle time: time spent in a particular stage.
  • Throughput: items completed over a period.
Example experiment
Rotate a reviewer for one sprint and set Review WIP to one. Measure average review cycle time before and after.
Interpreting signals
Many cards piling in one column is a clear signal of a bottleneck. Fewer started but more finished items show improved flow.
Misconception
Confusing busyness with progress. Busy teams may have low throughput; measure finished pieces instead of activity alone.
Why it matters
Flow measurement makes improvement decisions measurable and lowers the risk of changes that harm delivery.

screens.title: Make Process Policies Explicit
screens.subtitle: Reduce ambiguity by stating the rules for moving work

narration.text: Explicit policies clarify when work is ready to move between stages and reduce hidden handoffs. Without clear rules, only a few team members may know the implicit criteria, which creates confusion and delays. An explicit policy might state: a task moves to Testing only when code compiles, unit tests pass locally, and the creator has attached a test checklist. Writing these rules down removes guesswork and makes flow decisions teachable. A concrete example: a team documents an entry condition for QA—feature flagged, tests passing, and updated acceptance criteria. When a developer moves a card to QA, the tester can quickly verify the criteria rather than ask questions. A common misconception is treating explicit policies as rigid bureaucracy. In Kanban, policies are living hypotheses: write them, try them, and iterate based on feedback. The habit of codifying policy helps teams scale their shared understanding and makes responsibility for moving work clear. For classroom practice, draft one entry and one exit rule for a reviewer stage and use them for a sprint-long experiment to see if handoffs become faster and less disputed.

keyIdea.title: Explicit policies
keyIdea.text: Define clear entry/exit criteria to reduce ambiguity, speed handoffs, and enable reproducible flow.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Explicit Policies
Why policies matter

Explicit rules remove hidden knowledge and speed decision-making during handoffs.

Example policy
Move to QA only if code compiles, unit tests pass, and acceptance criteria are updated.
Activity
Draft one entry and one exit rule for a stage you use, then apply them for one sprint as an experiment.
How to use policies
  • Write concise, testable criteria.
  • Display policies near the board so anyone can read them.
  • Review and revise policies after experiments.
Key takeaway
Explicit policies convert tacit knowledge into shared rules that speed handoffs and support experiments.

screens.title: Implement Feedback Loops
screens.subtitle: Inspect delivery and customer outcomes regularly

narration.text: Feedback loops are the learning engine of Kanban. They create regular moments to inspect the system, review metrics, and adapt. Examples include short daily stand-ups focused on flow, service delivery reviews with customers, and operations reviews that analyze system-level performance. The purpose is to gather evidence and align on which experiments to run next. A concrete example: run a weekly flow stand-up where the team reviews cards blocked longer than a target and agrees on one immediate action to unblock them. Over time, collect lead time metrics and discuss trends in a monthly review. A common misconception is to equate more meetings with better feedback. Instead, each loop should have a clear purpose, a short agenda, and an output—a decision or experiment to test. For learners, start with a short daily check focused on blockages and WIP limits, then add a weekly review that looks at lead time and throughput. The discipline of scheduled inspection converts visible problems into actionable experiments and prevents recurring impediments from being forgotten. Implement Feedback Loops means short, purpose-driven reviews and metrics discussions create opportunities to inspect and adapt the system.. In practical terms, inspect delivery and customer outcomes regularly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Feedback loops
keyIdea.text: Short, purpose-driven reviews and metrics discussions create opportunities to inspect and adapt the system.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Feedback Loops
Types of loops
  • Daily flow stand-ups focused on blockages and WIP.
  • Service delivery reviews with stakeholders for outcomes.
  • Operations reviews to analyze system performance and metrics.
Example agenda
Daily: What’s blocking flow? Who needs help? What will we finish today? Output: one unblock action.
Practical guidance
  1. Keep loops short and purposeful.
  2. Always close with a decision or a small experiment.
  3. Record metrics so discussions are evidence-based.
Key takeaway
Design feedback loops that produce decisions and experiments, not just status updates.

screens.title: Improve Collaboratively, Evolve Experimentally
screens.subtitle: Use small experiments and data to drive change

narration.text: Improvement in Kanban is collaborative and experimental. Once you’ve visualized work, set limits, and collected flow data, propose one small change and test it. Examples of experiments include adjusting a WIP limit, changing who reviews work for one sprint, or clarifying a policy for moving items. The scientific approach is simple: state a hypothesis, choose a measurable metric like lead time or throughput, run the experiment for a fixed period, and compare results. A classroom activity ties this together: design a personal Kanban board with five tasks, set Doing WIP to two, simulate for two days, and measure how many tasks finish and their average lead time. Hypothesize that limiting WIP will reduce average lead time and increase completion rate. Run the short experiment and record observations. A common mistake is making multiple simultaneous changes, which makes it impossible to attribute results. Always change one variable at a time. The lasting insight is that small, repeatable experiments let teams learn safely and gradually evolve a better process that fits their context. Improve Collaboratively, Evolve Experimentally means run one small, measurable experiment at a time and use data to decide whether to adopt the change.. In practical terms, use small experiments and data to drive change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Experimentation
keyIdea.text: Run one small, measurable experiment at a time and use data to decide whether to adopt the change.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Improve & Experiment

Experiment design

A clear hypothesis, one variable, and a measurable outcome create useful learning.

Hypothesis
If we limit Doing WIP to two, average lead time will fall by the end of the week.
Metric
Average lead time for tasks; count of completed tasks per week.
Duration
Run the experiment for one sprint or a fixed number of days and record results.
Classroom activity
Design a personal board with To Do, Doing (WIP:2), Blocked, Done. Simulate moving cards and measure lead time for finished items.
Pitfall
Changing multiple variables at once prevents learning. Change one thing and measure.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the concise ideas to carry forward. First: Kanban is a flow method from lean manufacturing that makes work visible and limits WIP to reduce waste. Second: Flow, measured by lead time and throughput, is the primary indicator of delivery health—finish small items to learn quickly. Third: The Kanban practices—visualize workflow, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, and improve experimentally—form a suite that works together to create measurable improvements. Remember that Kanban is evolutionary, not revolutionary: start with what you do now, run small experiments, and respect existing roles. When you try this in practice, measure before and after, change one variable at a time, and use feedback loops to learn. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of adding boards without limits or making too many simultaneous changes. If you practice the simple personal board activity and one WIP experiment, you will have experienced the core mechanics of Kanban firsthand.

keyIdea.title: Essence
keyIdea.text: Kanban makes process visible, constrains work, and uses experiments to improve delivery.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts
Kanban
A method for managing work by visualizing flow and limiting concurrent items.
Work In Progress (WIP)
The number of items actively worked on; limits reduce multitasking and improve throughput.
Flow
The smooth movement of items through stages; measured by lead time and throughput.
Summary takeaway
Use visualization, WIP limits, and small experiments to convert overload into measurable, improvable workflow.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to guide your first experiments

narration.text: Keep three simple reminders as you begin using Kanban. First: start where you are—don’t discard existing roles; map them and test changes incrementally. Second: limit WIP and treat limits as experiments; they are hypotheses about capacity, not arbitrary rules. Third: measure and use feedback loops—collect lead time and throughput data, run a focused review, and design one small experiment. These reminders help you avoid common traps: changing too much at once, adding a board without limits, or running meetings without clear outcomes. If you follow these three rules, you can rapidly iterate on process improvements while keeping the team stable and engaged. Try one small experiment this week and measure a single metric; the result will teach you more than theoretical advice alone. What to Remember means start small, limit wip, measure results—one experiment at a time.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to guide your first experiments. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Start small, limit WIP, measure results—one experiment at a time.

Start where you are
Map current flow and make changes that respect existing roles and knowledge.
Limit WIP
Set a WIP cap as an experiment to reveal capacity and reduce multitasking.
Measure & experiment
Collect lead time and throughput, run one small experiment, and decide by data.
Final thought
Kanban helps you turn hidden process problems into visible opportunities for safe, measured improvement.
